Re: Appeal of Adverse Benefit Determination

Reference Number: POC-C65CA65DA3-33163
Date of Notice: 2026-08-24
Service: Hip arthroscopy, CPT 29914
Appeal Deadline: 2027-02-20

To the Aetna Appeals Committee:

I am writing to appeal the denial of prior authorization for hip arthroscopy (CPT 29914), as set forth in the Notice of Adverse Benefit Determination dated 2026-08-24 (reference POC-C65CA65DA3-33163). The stated reason for denial was that "the clinical records submitted do not document an adequate trial of conservative treatment prior to the requested surgery." I respectfully disagree and ask that Aetna reverse this determination based on the medical necessity criteria in Aetna's own Clinical Policy Bulletin Number 736, and on the clinical record summarized below.

Aetna's Clinical Policy Bulletin 0736 states that femoro-acetabular surgery, open or arthroscopic, is medically necessary for persons who fulfill all of the following criteria, and I address each in turn:

1. Imaging showing FAI with labral pathology and cam, pincer, or pistol-grip morphology.

CPB 0736 requires: "Diagnosis of definite femoro-acetabular impingement (FAI) defined by appropriate imaging studies (X-rays, MRI or CT scans), showing labral pathology (e.g. partial or full thickness labral tearing or labral damage) with one or more of the following: cam impingement (alpha angle greater than 50 degrees) pincer impingement (acetabular retroversion or coxa profunda) (center edge angle greater than or equal to 40 degrees), or pistol grip deformity (non-spherical femoral head shape)."

MRI arthrogram of the hip on 2026-07-11 documents an anterosuperior labral tear with cam-type femoroacetabular impingement and an alpha angle of 68 degrees, which exceeds the 50-degree threshold. This criterion is met.

2. Duration and severity of symptoms.

CPB 0736 requires: "Moderate to severe symptoms typical of FAI (hip or groin pain that is worsened by flexion activities (e.g., squatting or prolonged sitting) that significantly limits activities, with duration of at least 6 months."

The patient has had 24 months of progressive hip pain, unrelieved by rest, with sharp anterior groin pain on sitting and pivoting, and an inability to run or squat. This far exceeds the 6-month minimum and matches the flexion/prolonged-sitting pattern described in the policy.

3. Positive impingement sign.

CPB 0736 requires: "Positive impingement sign with sudden pain on 90 degree hip flexion with adduction and internal rotation or extension and external rotation."

The physical exam documents positive provocative testing on the affected side with pain-limited range of motion. [Please confirm with the enclosed exam note whether the specific 90-degree flexion/adduction/internal-rotation maneuver was performed and documented, as the summary provided does not specify the exact maneuver.]

4. Failure of conservative treatment.

This is the specific basis cited for denial, so I address it in detail. CPB 0736 requires: "Failure to respond to all available conservative treatment options including: activity modification (e.g., restriction of athletic pursuits and avoidance of symptomatic motion), pharmacological intervention (e.g., non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs [NSAIDS]), injections of local anesthetics into the joint) and physiotherapy. The treatment should be for at least 12 weeks in the past year with at least 6 weeks being formal physiotherapy (in-person with a licensed physical therapist not virtual). Physical therapy (PT) needs to be confirmed either by the actual PT notes, or by documentation in the member claims history."

The record demonstrates all of the required modalities, each exceeding the minimum duration specified:

- Physiotherapy: Supervised, in-person physical therapy focused on core and hip stabilization with activity modification, 14 weeks (2026-04-27 through 2026-08-03), 18 completed visits, documented in the physical therapy discharge note. This is more than double the 6-week minimum of formal physiotherapy required by the policy, and the total conservative-care window (14 weeks) exceeds the 12-week minimum stated in the policy.
- Activity modification: The PT program specifically included activity modification, and the patient's functional record shows restriction from running and squatting due to pain.
- Pharmacological intervention: NSAIDs were used for 8 months with inadequate relief.
- Injection therapy: A corticosteroid injection was administered on 2026-06-14, giving 4 weeks of partial relief. [Note: CPB 0736's text specifies "injections of local anesthetics into the joint"; the injection documented in this record was corticosteroid rather than a local anesthetic. If Aetna's medical necessity determination requires an anesthetic-specific injection, please advise, and Dr. Okafor can address whether an anesthetic injection is clinically appropriate or whether the corticosteroid injection satisfies the intent of this criterion.]

Taken together, the record shows 14 weeks of formal, in-person, supervised physical therapy (more than twice the required 6 weeks), 8 months of NSAID therapy, activity modification, and an intra-articular corticosteroid injection with only transient benefit — all within the past year. This is a complete and well-documented trial of conservative treatment that, in my reading of Aetna's own published criteria, satisfies the requirement Aetna cited as the basis for denial. I am enclosing the physical therapy discharge note, medication history, and injection record to support this timeline.

5. Absence of advanced osteoarthritis or joint space narrowing.

CPB 0736 requires: "Absence of advanced osteoarthritis change on pre-operative X-ray (Tonnis grade 2 or more) or severe cartilage injury (Outerbridge grade III or IV)" and "Absence of joint space narrowing on plain radiograph of the pelvis. Joint space is not less than 2 mm wide anywhere along the sourcil."

The MRI arthrogram of 2026-07-11 documents Tonnis grade 0 and preserved joint space. Both criteria are met.

6. Absence of joint laxity syndromes and osteogenesis imperfecta; other causes of hip pain ruled out.

CPB 0736 also requires that "Member does not have generalized joint laxity especially in diseases connected with hypermobility of the joints, such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome," that the "Member does not have osteogenesis imperfecta," and that "All other potential sources of hip pain have been ruled out." [The clinical summary provided to me does not contain an explicit statement addressing these three items. Dr. Okafor's office should supplement the appeal record with a brief statement confirming the absence of these conditions and confirming that other sources of hip pain have been excluded, if not already documented in the chart.]

Conclusion

Based on the criteria published in Aetna's own Clinical Policy Bulletin 0736 and the clinical documentation summarized above — including 24 months of symptoms, 14 weeks of formal in-person physical therapy (18 visits), 8 months of NSAID use, a corticosteroid injection with only transient benefit, MRI-confirmed cam FAI with an alpha angle of 68 degrees and a labral tear, Tonnis grade 0, and positive provocative testing — the stated basis for denial (inadequate trial of conservative treatment) is not supported by the record. I ask that Aetna reverse the denial and authorize hip arthroscopy (CPT 29914) for this member.

I have enclosed the following records in support of this appeal:
- Physical therapy discharge note (2026-04-27 to 2026-08-03)
- Medication/NSAID treatment history
- Corticosteroid injection record (2026-06-14)
- MRI arthrogram report (2026-07-11)
- Physical examination note documenting provocative testing
- [Surgeon's letter of medical necessity from Dr. Okafor, if not already on file]

Please confirm receipt of this appeal and provide written notice of Aetna's determination within the timeframe required under the plan and applicable law. If you require any additional documentation, please contact [provider's office contact name/phone] or me directly at [phone/email].

Thank you for your prompt attention to this matter.

Sincerely,

Taylor Foster
